The Hooded mountain tanager (Buthraupis montana) is a striking high-altitude passerine inhabiting the páramo and cloud forest zones of the northern Andes. Field-based monitoring of breeding pairs in the Cordillera Central of Colombia has revealed several key life-history parameters. Eggs are incubated at a steady temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], with the nestlings emerging after an incubation period of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a value consistent with the developmental rates of other large-bodied Thraupidae. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings have an initial wet body mass of just 12 grams [Ww0 = 12 grams], reflecting the relatively energy-limited yolk reserves typical of montane songbirds. This modest starting weight underscores the considerable parental investment required during the subsequent nestling phase, as the chicks must undergo rapid somatic growth to reach independence in a short window dictated by the abbreviated tropical breeding season.

Under the typical thermal conditions experienced during the active metabolic period of this species, which center on a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the developmental milestones proceed in a predictable sequence. The time elapsed from hatching to fledging, when the nestlings achieve their first sustained flight, is 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid transition from a dependent nestling to a fledgling capable of short-distance movement is exceptionally brief, even among altricial tropical passerines, and may represent an adaptation to reduce the risk of nest predation in the exposed, paramo-edge habitats the species favors. The pin-feathered chicks develop their juvenile plumage quickly, and by the time of nest departure they are already capable of clumsy flight, though they continue to be provisioned by the parents for a subsequent period.

Following the fledging period, the young birds enter a pre-reproductive juvenile stage. The onset of puberty, defined by the maturation of the gonads and the initiation of gametogenesis, occurs at an age of 33 days after hatching [tp = 33 days after hatching] when measured at the species' typical active body temperature of 40.2 °C at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This represents a relatively early attainment of sexual maturity for a bird of this body size, and it suggests that the species may invest in early reproductive potential rather than extended somatic growth. The juveniles begin to develop adult-like plumage characteristics around this time, and they start to show exploratory behavior and territorial interactions with conspecifics, which are precursors to the establishment of a breeding territory in subsequent years.

The first successful breeding event, or the time since birth at first brood, is deferred until approximately 1.6 years after hatching [tR = approximately 1.6 years after hatching] when maintained at the typical body temperat at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]ure of 40.2 °C. This delay between reaching puberty and initiating reproduction suggests that young birds require an extended period to acquire sufficient body condition and to secure a high-quality territory in the competitive social environment of the páramo. During this period, the subadult birds continue to gain mass, ultimately reaching an adult female body mass of approximately 102 grams [Wwi = approximately 102 grams], which represents a substantial increase from the 12 grams at hatching. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is 12.2 years [am = 12.2 years] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which is notable among montane tanagers.

Reproductive output is modest, consistent with the life-history strategy of a long-lived, high-altitude specialist. Females typically lay a clutch of 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nesting attempt], and field observations indicate they produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This annual reproductive rate is among the lowest recorded for Thraupidae and likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the cold, oxygen-poor environment of the páramo. The maximum basal metabolic rate, measured as oxygen consumption under resting conditions, has been recorded at 185.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 185.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the bird's body temperature is held at 40.2 °C, a rate that is notably elevated for a passerine of this mass and reflects the high metabolic cost of thermoregulation in the cold, hypoxic páramo at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This elevated metabolic demand, combined with the low reproductive output, illustrates a classic slow-paced life history adapted to stable, resource-limited high-altitude environments.
